narrative:
The model predicted a 61% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven by three key factors, ranked by importance. Your class rank at the end of your third year was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction toward failure. You placed in the third decile, noticeably lower than the average of roughly sixth decile among students who were accepted. This signal of relative academic standing in law school carried the most weight.

Next, your LSAT score of 33 also pulled the prediction toward failure. It sits below the average of 37 among accepted applicants, adding further concern about readiness for the bar.

Working in the opposite direction, your undergraduate GPA of 3.9 was the third most important factor and worked in your favor. It is substantially higher than the 3.23 average of accepted students and helped offset some of the risk.

Taken together, the model concluded that the combination of lower law-school performance and a below-average LSAT outweighed your strong college grades.

What you should do next is straightforward: focus on improving your bar-exam readiness. Consider a structured bar-prep course, practice exams, or additional study time before retaking the exam. Once you have a stronger first-time pass probability, you can reapply with a much better chance of admission.
